title: Everyone's Talking About It
companyContext: A small specialty-chemicals company. Over the past few weeks its share price has shot up after a viral social-media post calling it 'the next big thing'. You don't own it, and you're wondering whether to jump in.

stages.note: Revenue growth of +3% vs last year (it grew +18% the year before) means the company is still growing, just far more slowly than before. A profit margin of 4.1% (down from 9.8%) means it keeps less profit from every ₹100 of sales than it used to. A P/E of 85, versus 22 for similar companies, means investors are paying about four times what they pay for its peers, for every ₹1 of yearly profit. These figures are from the most recent quarter - the price started rising several weeks before any of this came out.

stages.headline: "Retail trading forums buzzing: 'this stock could 10x' - trading volume 6x normal"
stages.note: Almost all of that extra buying volume has shown up in just the last week.
The price has kept climbing since the buzz began.

choices.label: Wait for more information
choices.description: Wait for the next results or more evidence.

criteria.description: Notices that revenue growth and margins are deteriorating even as the price rallies.
Doesn't treat social-media buzz or a volume surge on its own as a reason to buy.
Flags that the P/E is far above the sector average without pointing to a fundamental reason for it.

factorOptions.label: Revenue growth and profit margins have both gotten worse even as the price keeps climbing
The rally is being driven by social-media buzz and a volume spike, not a change in the business
The P/E is far above the sector average with no fundamental improvement to justify it
The stock has more than doubled in a few weeks

rubric.idealSummary: When the price is climbing but revenue growth and margins are shrinking, the price and the business are telling opposite stories - and the price is usually the one that's wrong. A P/E four times the peer average, with no improvement in the business to justify it, means you'd be paying up purely because a crowd is excited. Buying momentum isn't always wrong, but buying it without noticing that the fundamentals are sliding underneath is a bet on the crowd staying excited, not an investment.

outcome.summary: The rally lasted a little longer, then the next results confirmed the weak numbers and the excitement faded. The stock gave back the entire move and more over a few weeks.

survivorshipNote: Represents a hype-driven small-cap rally that fully round-trips and then some - the dataset needs at least one clear speculative-bubble unwind, not just gradual declines.
